realLife: Single-cell biology and embedding inspection lean on t-SNE and UMAP plots, which is also where they get misread most.
summary: Squash many dimensions to a flat map that keeps neighbours together, and learn what the map cannot tell you.
headline: A map that keeps friends close and lies about the rest
overview: t-SNE turns distances into probabilities of being neighbours, then arranges points on a plane so that the neighbour pattern matches. It is good at showing which points belong together.

It is bad at everything else. Cluster sizes, gaps between clusters and the overall layout are not reliable. Perplexity, roughly how many neighbours each point counts, changes the picture a lot. UMAP, covered below the widget, plays a similar game with a different loss.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Drop perplexity to 2. The map shatters real groups into small fake clumps. The size comparison shows a cluster three times wider can be drawn at nearly the same size.

check.question: Which of these can you trust in a t-SNE plot?
options: Which points sit near each other
How far apart two clusters are

data: Ninety points in 8 dimensions drawn as three Gaussian groups, one tight and one wide. The widget runs exact t-SNE in your browser. It does not run UMAP: that part of the lesson is explained, not demonstrated.
maths: $$p_{j\mid i}=\frac{\exp(-\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2/2\sigma_i^2)}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp(-\lVert x_i-x_k\rVert^2/2\sigma_i^2)},\qquad p_{ij}=\frac{p_{j\mid i}+p_{i\mid j}}{2n}$$
Each σ_i is tuned so the spread of its neighbour weights matches the chosen perplexity.

Kobak and Linderman found UMAP with random starting positions preserves global layout as poorly as t-SNE does, and that t-SNE started from PCA does about as well as UMAP. Other guides still say UMAP keeps more global structure. Treat that claim as contested.
code:
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
Y = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init='pca', random_state=0).fit_transform(X)
